paper_title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imagery

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.

sections.content: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellites data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellites data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change. 1. Introduction Multimodal agents now open files, write code, and carry out multi-step data analysis with tools [6, 31, 32, 35, 70]. Turning the Earths fifty-year satellite record [10, 65] into reliable land-change analysistracking forest loss, surface water, settlements, and fire [22, 27, 4547]is both central task of Earth observation science and demanding test of these agents. In practice, such analysis begins not with clean RGB image, but with decades of observations distributed across multiple satellite missions, where an analyst must screen clouds and gaps, map transitions from imagery, and harmonize measurements across sensors and across years [7, 41, 48, 50]. Whether multimodal agents can carry out these analyses end to end remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short in both the data they provide and what their scores verify (Tab. 1). Visionlanguage [5, 36, 64] and remote-sensing multimodal benchmarks [2, 66, 68] pose questions on curated images, and recent Earth-observation agent benchmarks [19, 33, 38, 44, 51, 61, 72] still hand agents preprocessed inputs or shortterm tasks, or let them fetch data through dedicated tools, leaving out the raw, multi-decadal, multi-sensor archives where land-change analysis begins. Moreover, scoring the final answer alone does not verify how the agent reached it. Models often answer about region from prior knowledge without using the data [1, 5, 36, 63, 67]. Even when an agent computes from the recorded pixels, sensor measures radiance that depends on the atmosphere, viewing geometry, and instrument as well as on the ground [41, 50]. In the satellite record, sensor shifts have repeatedly created apparent changes on Earth: tropospheric cooling from orbital decay [62], vegetation browning from degrading sensor [60, 75], and an Amazon green-up from viewing geometry [42]. Each time the pixel values moved, the question was whether the ground had changed [7, 15, 18, 48]. We introduce EarthRecord, benchmark that evaluates whether multimodal agents can turn four decades of raw satellite records into reliable land-change analysis  (Fig. 1)  . In an offline sandbox with Python, shell, and an image viewer, an agent receives the record of site as distributed [10]unscaled single-band rasters from Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 spanning 1984 2026 across 56 sitesleaving cloud masking, mapping, and cross-sensor harmonization to the agent. EarthRecord poses 238 questions across ten analysis tasks (153 computable from the record, 73 asking what is on the ground, and 12 with insufficient evidence), scored by pass3 across three passes against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record to measure what prior knowledge alone can answer, and instrument pairs alter one satellites data while nothing changes on the ground, testing cross-sensor checks. Evaluating twelve multimodal agents on EarthRecord reveals both their end-to-end capability and two fundamental bottlenecks (Fig. 1c, d). First, the four leading agents complete most analyses end to endscoring 81.0% to 85.4% pass3 on the 226 computable and recognition questions but the six leading models drop from 92.0% on questions computed from record variables to 61.1% on those requiring map from imagery, where runs often abstain early, mostly without viewing an image, or judge inconsistently across passes (Sec. 3). Second, the controls show that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels, but not yet to the ground (Sec. 4). Providing the record lifts all twelve models on computable questions, though regional priors persist on recognition questions. When one satellites data are altered in instrument pairs, however, 53.5% of right answers turn wrong and follow the altered pixels, and few failed runs attribute the break to the instrument. Our contributions are three. benchmark on the raw satellite record. We show that leading agents complete most variable-computed analyses end to end but falter at mapping from imagery, and half of right answers follow altered sensors. 2. EarthRecord Each EarthRecord question asks about the land surface at given site over given period. In an offline sandbox (Sec. 2.4 and Sec. A), the agent receives the sites raw record as distributed by its providersleaving data selection, cloud masking, scaling, mapping, and cross-sensor harmonization to the agentand submits structured answer scored against verifiable references under the standard evaluation and two controls. 2.1. Sites and the raw record EarthRecord spans 56 sites: 48 core areas of 1030 km on side and 8 administrative regions [49]. The core areas cover eight themes, with six areas each, across six continents and all five Koppen climate groups [3], selected by screening global grid for thematic signal and then reviewed manually. To probe how prior knowledge interacts with the data, they include 8 famous areas, 7 stable areas selected for their lack of significant change, and 33 obscure areas; the agent can read each areas coordinates. The record combines four decades of observations up to its snapshot date of 30 September 2026  (Fig. 2)  . Landsat surface reflectance begins in 1984, spans TM, ETM+, and OLI [10], and provides median of 1,101 scenes per core area; 109 of the 238 questions span two or more of these Landsat sensors (Fig. 2a). MODIS vegetation indices, land surface temperature, and snow cover begin in 2000 on Terra and later Aqua [1114, 25, 26, 58, 59], and VIIRS vegetation indices and temperature begin in 2012 [28, 57]. Sentinel-2 surface reflectance enters in 2019 with at most one scene per month [16], and processing baselines from 2022 add radiometric offset [9]. ERA5-Land reanalysis [8, 43], global land cover [20, 73, 74], terrain [17], and administrative boundaries complete the record, and the regions have no Landsat or Sentinel-2 data. Apart from the regional boundary mask and the instrument pairs (Sec. 2.5), pixel values are unmodified: scale factors, offsets, and quality layers are not applied, and README gives the conversions. Duplicate and at least 90% obscured scenes are removed, and archive issues present as distributed are kept: of the 57,157 Landsat scenes over the core areas, 4,485 are Tier 2 [56], with geometric offsets of up to 15.7 km, and quality layers missed cloud in 5 of 200 sampled scenes they rated clear. 2.2. Questions and analysis tasks The benchmark poses 238 questions207 at core areas across eight themes (forest, greening, agriculture, water, urban, fire, snow, and coast) and 31 at the regionsover periods of 1 to 38 years. Every question specifies structured answer fields, including designated conclusion field used for scoring, and every field accepts insufficient evidence. Each question belongs to one of ten analysis tasks set by its template (Sec. B.1): Quantify (49), Trend (28), Date (26), Compare (24), Regional statistics (21), Attribute (20), Anomaly and climate (19), Detect (16), Season (12), and Recovery (11), counted over the 226 computable and recognition questions. Figure 2. The record spans changing instruments. (a) Sensor coverage in the record, with hatching after the 2003 Landsat 7 scan-line corrector failure. (b) True-color crops of one site on the dates marked 14, with the same extent and reflectance stretch. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2024. Landsat data courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey. Figure 3. One example question per class. Questions are shortened, and bold text gives the reference answer. (ac) Two Landsat scenes of one site, with the same extent and reflectance stretch within each pair. (d) Landsat scenes per year at one site, with the question period in gray. Landsat data courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey. Questions fall into three classes, assigned from the target variable. Computable questions (153, including all 31 regional questions) ask for quantities that formula can derive from the record, such as greenness trends, lake-area trends, or snow-cover days (Fig. 3a). Recognition questions (73, of which 50 are in the forest, fire, and urban themes) ask what is on the ground or what happened, such as forest loss, burn scars, built-up expansion, or coastal reclamation (41 with product references and 32 with visual references; Fig. 3b, c). Insufficient-evidence questions (12) cover periods with too few clear observations to support conclusion (Fig. 3d). 2.3. Reference answers The target quantity determines the source of each reference answer. First, the 98 computable questions without global product take references derived from variables in the record: several methods compute each quantity, numeric references take the method median, and categorical and date conclusions require at least 75% of methods to agree. Reference methods use Tier 1 Landsat scenes with bright-cloud pixels removed, and the 66 questions that rely on Landsat methods reach the same conclusions with and without this step. Second, 13 questions take their reference from global products included in the record. Third, 78 questions take their reference from four global products withheld from the record: Hansen forest loss [27], JRC surface water [45], GHSL built-up surface [46], and MCD64A1 burned area [22]. To answer these 41 recognition and 37 computable questions (such as the lake-area trend in Fig. 3a), the agent must map the change from the imagery itself. Fourth, causes and landcover types, and cases where products and methods diverge widely, are set by human review of AI-drafted visual interpretations of the imagery (37 questions: 32 recognition and 5 computable). The 12 insufficient-evidence questions are set by the number of observations and the clear-sky fraction in the queried period. numeric answer is right when it falls within the reference range, which 159 questions derive from product and method results and which spans at least 5% of the reference value. Decision thresholds are stated in the question text, and questions with results close to threshold were replaced during construction. 2.4. Protocol and scoring Each run uses fresh, offline, CPU-only container with 4 CPUs and 24 GB of memory, Python, shell, geospatial and classical machine-learning libraries, and an image viewer. Because the record is delivered as single-band raster files and the viewer reads rendered images, an agent must select bands, apply stretch, and render an image before it can inspect it. All models share the same system prompt and tools, each run is limited to 3,600 of working time and 300 messages, and each answer is submitted with confidence 4 and method summary with caveats. Every question is run for three passes and scored on its conclusion field by pass3 [71], which is 1 when the conclusion is right in all three passes and 0 otherwise. Intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals over questions, and the baselines are the majority class and an always-no-change answer, which is the reference answer for 32 questions. The first models run served as pilot check of the bank: after its results, references were audited and corrected across the entire bank by question-type rules, 11 questions with unstable references were removed, and pass3 was set as the main score. Because question texts did not change, that model was rescored rather than rerun, and the other eleven models ran on the frozen bank. 2.5. Controls Two controls test what the conclusions rest on. Closed-book runs give the model the same question and the sites bounding box without the record, and measure what prior knowledge alone can answer; the difference from the score with the record is the gain from the record (Tab. 4). Instrument pairs alter one satellites data in the record while nothing changes on the ground, and score the answer against the original question and reference answer. All 22 pairs use computable questions: 21 scale one satellites values from 2018 onward, by up to 20% in 20 pairs and by 5% in one, and the remaining pair replaces Landsat 8 scenes from 20132017 with Landsat 7 scenes. Every retained pair is detectable by comparison with concurrent satellites, and the alteration changes the conclusion of reference method that relies on the affected satellite. Eight placebo pairs remove 5% of clear scenes at random and measure conclusion variability unrelated to the instrument. Modelpair cases right on the original in all three passes are sorted by the altered version: moved cases turn wrong, held cases stay right but are already right in the closed book or have no change as the reference, and beyond cases stay right otherwise (Sec. 4.2). 3. C.5). 5. Related work Remote sensing vision-language models and benchmarks. Remote sensing vision-language models answer questions on single scenes, in dialogues, and over image time series [29, 34, 53], and their benchmarks use curated imagery [2, 21, 66, 68]. Robustness benchmarks test foundation models under corruptions and shifts, including radiometric gain and change of sensor [15, 18, 37]. EarthRecord evaluates decades of raw record at one site instead of scene. Agents for data analysis and Earth observation. Sandbox agents are scored by their results in software engineering, databases, and data science [6, 31, 32, 35], and in vision, models write programs to answer visual questions [24, 54]. Earth observation agents call tools for retrieval, spectral indices, change detection, or disaster assessment [19, 33, 44, 51, 61, 72], industrial systems combine them with geospatial foundation models [4, 52], and Earth-Agent-Pro [38] lets them acquire observations through tools, without controls for prior knowledge or sensor shifts. EarthRecord gives the agent each sites multisensor archive as distributed, with withheld references and three passes per question. Controls for prior knowledge and sensor shifts. Models can answer visual questions without the image [1, 23, 30], so benchmarks add blind controls [5, 21, 69] or run agents without tools or internet access [19, 33]. Language models hold extractable but biased geographic knowledge [39, 40], and studies measure how they weigh it against external evidence [63, 67]. The closed book of EarthRecord follows this line, and its instrument pairs follow paired counterfactual tests [36, 55] and sensor changes [15, 18] but alter the data the agent itself processes Figure 6. With the record, answers shift from prior knowledge to the pixels. When the pixels are altered, however, the answers shift with them rather than reflecting change on the ground. The question in Fig. 1a illustrates this sequence. 4.1. From prior knowledge to the pixels In Fig. 1a, the question asks whether greenness at stable forest in northern Argentina has changed significantly. In the closed book, GPT-6 Sol answers decrease, reasoning that clearing in the region usually lowers greenness; with the record, it computes from the pixels and finds no significant trend, in agreement with the reference. The same shift from prior knowledge to the pixels holds for all twelve models: with the record, they score 4.6 to 60.8 points higher on computable questions (Tab. 4), and far more answers turn from wrong to right than from right to wrong, 40.9% of modelquestion pairs against 5.8% (Sec. C.1). On recognition questions, by contrast, the record contributes less and prior knowledge persists. With the record, four models score lower on recognition questions than in the closed book (Tab. 4). Even for the three leading models, recognition answers barely depend on viewing the imagery: without the image tool, they give almost the same answers (Sec. C.2). At famous areas, prior knowledge outperforms the record: the closed book scores 55.9 and the record 50.0 (Sec. C.3). 4.2. To the pixels, but not yet to the ground When one satellites data change, the answers change with them. In Fig. 1a, Terra NDVI is scaled down from 2018 onward while nothing changes on the ground, yet GPT-6 Sol now answers decrease. The pattern is general: 53.5% of the cases right on the original turn wrong after the alteration (74/102 on Terra NDVI, 20/50 on Landsat 8, and 13/48 on Terra snow), 91% of the changed answers move in the direction of the alteration, and answers on placebo pairs change 8 while the ground stays as it is. 6. Conclusion EarthRecord evaluates whether multimodal agents can turn four decades of raw, multi-sensor satellite records into reliable land-change analysis across 56 sites and 238 questions. Across twelve agents, the bottleneck lies not in executing code over the archive but in two scientific steps: mapping change from the imagery and verifying whether change in the pixels reflects change on the ground. Leading agents complete most variable-computed analyses end to end, yet falter when question requires mapsome abstaining, mostly without viewing an image, and others judging inconsistently across passes. When one satellites data are altered in stress-test instrument pairs, 53.5% of right answers follow the altered sensor while only 3.5% of failed runs blame the instrument. Because our sandbox provides general geospatial and classical machine-learning libraries on CPU and our instrument pairs test clear-cut breaks, equipping agents with pretrained vision models for mapping and with routine cross-sensor checks for subtle drift are natural next steps. EarthRecord and its evaluation sandbox will be released.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: Multimodal agents are the subjects evaluated in this benchmark (Secs. 3 and 4). In addition, large language models (Claude and GPT) were used in three supporting roles under the authors verification: (1) drafting initial visual interpretations for the 37 visual-reference questions, all of which were reviewed and verified by the authors (Sec. 2.3); (2) coding failure steps across 144 sampled wrong runs (Sec. B.8) and sensor-reporting behaviors across 273 instrument-pair runs (Sec. C.5) from the submitted method summaries and caveats, where author checks on 36 and 31 runs respectively showed full agreement; and (3) assisting with analysis and plotting scripts, reference formatting, and language editing of the manuscript. All scientific claims, analyses, code, and final text were verified by the authors.
